facts.statement: The extinct songbird genus Palaeoscinis was described in 1957 from fossils found in the middle Miocene Monterey Formation of Santa Barbara, California.
facts.quote: Palaeoscinis (meaning "ancient oscine") is an extinct genus of songbird described in 1957 from the middle Miocene of the Monterey Formation in Santa Barbara, California.

facts.statement: The fossil was discovered in 1955 on limestone slabs that were originally intended to be used as flagstones.
facts.quote: The fossil was first discovered in 1955 on two slabs of limestone intended for use as flagstones before being recognised for their significance.

facts.statement: The species name turdirostris was chosen because the bird had a beak shape similar to that of a thrush.
facts.quote: The specific name was chosen for the thrush-like shape of its beak.

facts.statement: Palaeoscinis had a long, slender beak and body proportions similar to the modern varied thrush.
facts.quote: The beak is long and slender, similar to that of the modern varied thrush, and its body proportions are also generally similar to thrushes.

facts.statement: Unlike modern thrushes, Palaeoscinis had relatively short legs that were shorter than its wing bones.
facts.quote: The legs are relatively short, though, unlike thrushes, and are shorter than the bones of the wing.

facts.statement: The claw on the reversed first toe was long, measuring approximately 70% of the length of the preceding toe bone.
facts.quote: The claw of the reversed 1st toe is long, approximately 70% the length of the preceding toe bone.

facts.statement: Palaeoscinis was placed in its own family due to unique skeletal characteristics of the sternum, shoulder, and humerus, as well as proportions unlike any known songbird family.
facts.quote: Palaeoscinus was assigned to its own family due to the combination of skeletal characteristics (mostly of the sternum, shoulder, and humerus) and its proportions being unlike any modern or fossil family of songbirds.

facts.statement: Palaeoscinis lived during the Langhian to Serravallian stages, from 15.98 to 11.63 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Langhian to Serravallian (15.98 to 11.63 million years ago)

facts.statement: Howard (1957) suggested Palaeoscinis might be related to bulbuls, waxwings, corvids, or dippers, though this relationship is not certain.
facts.quote: However, it was regarded as similar and possibly related to the Pycnonotidae (bulbuls), Bombycillidae (waxwings), Corvidae, or Cinclidae (dippers) by Howard (1957).

facts.statement: Wetmore (1960) provisionally allocated Palaeoscinis as closest to the Pycnonotidae based on proportions, although this relationship remains uncertain.
facts.quote: It was provisionally allocated as closest to the Pycnonotidae over the other families by Wetmore (1960) based on its proportions, although this relationship is not certain.

rejected.statement: Although found in marine sediments, the anatomy of Palaeoscinis indicates it was a songbird rather than a seabird.
rejected.quote: The fossil was found in marine sediments, but the anatomy of Palaeoscinis indicates that it was a songbird rather than a seabird.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'it was a songbird rather than a seabird'

rejected.statement: Palaeoscinis belongs to the extinct monotypic family Palaeoscinidae and contains only one species, P. turdirostris.
rejected.quote: It is assigned to the extinct monotypic family Palaeoscinidae, and contains the type and only species P. turdirostris.
